title: Semmelweis introduces handwashing at Vienna General Hospital
summary: In 1847 at Vienna General Hospital, the Hungarian physician Ignaz Semmelweis concluded that cadaverous particles on doctors' hands from the morgue were causing deadly fever in mothers at the First Clinic. He required students and doctors to wash their hands in a chlorinated lime solution before patient contact. Reported mortality fell from about 18% to under 2%. He is called the father of hand hygiene.

uncertainty.note: Sources date the handwashing rule to 1847.

as_recorded.value: in 1847, the mortality rate of the First Clinic was 18.27%, whereas, in 1848, it had precipitously dropped to 1.27%

In 1847 Semmelweis demonstrated that the mortality rate among mothers delivering at the First Obstetrics Clinic at the General Hospital of Vienna was significantly lower when hospital staff cleaned their hands with an antiseptic agent

importance.justification: Showed that hand antisepsis could sharply cut deaths from childbed fever, before germ theory was accepted.
